tagline: Gravel beside Steens Mountain leads past salt flats to Fields.
intro: The East Steens Tour Route follows the mountain’s eastern escarpment and the Alvord Desert for 143 miles. Oregon DOT presents this Tour Route in its scenic-byways program as a study in contrasts, with five to seven hours of minimum driving time. Part of the drive is gravel, with Steens Mountain to the west and desert salt flats to the east. Steens rises a vertical mile from the Alvord Basin to nearly 10,000 feet, giving the road a mountain face on one side of the desert.

The highway portion acquired its number in 1932, when Oregon assigned Route 78 to the Burns-Crane Highway. Travel beside the Alvord once took a different course: in a 1977 oral history, George Renwick recalled drivers crossing the dry playa toward Mosquito Creek before a road was built along the basin’s edge. The mountain-side stretch of East Steens Road is county-maintained gravel.

From Burns, take Route 78 southeast through Crane and New Princeton. Near milepost 65, the tour turns onto East Steens Road. The sagebrush-covered Sheepshead Mountains lie east of the road before a series of small lakes, which can be dry depending on the year. Mann Lake comes next, then the Alvord salt flats, before the route ends at Fields.

moments.title: Crane
moments.text: The town takes its name from Crane Creek and Crane Creek Gap, a pass between the Harney Basin and the South Fork Malheur River’s drainage basin. Crane’s post office reopened when the Union Pacific Railroad arrived from Ontario in 1916. Until the line reached Burns in 1924, the town was an important livestock shipping point, supporting four hotels, five restaurants and a dance hall. A series of fires, the last in 1938, preceded a lasting loss of prosperity. Crane Union High School serves a large rural district as a boarding school.

moments.title: Alvord Desert
moments.text: The Alvord’s salt surface records water arriving and disappearing. Streams reach the playa at Steens Mountain’s eastern foot, but the basin has no outlet; evaporation leaves minerals behind. Faulting lowered the basin that holds this dry lake. During the late Pleistocene, a much larger lake covered the playa, reaching more than 80 miles in length and up to 280 feet deep. About 13,000 years ago, the larger lake breached Big Sand Gap, sending several cubic miles of water into the Coyote Lake basin. The playa can flood in wet periods, but it is dry for much of the year.
moments.notice: Salt minerals remain on the playa after water evaporates.

moments.title: Fields
moments.text: Ranching in the Fields area began in 1869 with the establishment of Whitehorse Ranch. Charles Fields settled here in 1881 and built a roadhouse serving the route between Winnemucca and Burns. A one-room school was established around 1900, with a single teacher. He sold the business to John Smyth in 1911; the post office followed two years later. The stone roadhouse was remodeled into a store and restaurant and remains in use. The surrounding ranches use Fields as a center of commerce. A school, campground and a few houses are part of the community at the tour’s end.
